claims.claim: An email address has two parts joined by an @ sign: a local-part identifying the mailbox and a domain naming the mail system, written local-part@domain.
SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) is the standard used to submit and transfer outgoing mail between mail servers.
IMAP lets a client access and manage messages that remain stored on the server, so the same mailbox stays in sync across multiple devices.
POP3 is designed to download mail from the server to one device, and in its typical mode the message is then deleted from the server.
A message carries header fields including From, To, Cc, Bcc, Subject, and Date, plus a body. Addresses on To and Cc are visible to all recipients.

Bcc (blind carbon copy) recipients receive the message without their addresses being shown to the other recipients; RFC 5322 describes handling where the Bcc line is removed from the copies other recipients receive.

Phishing messages try to get the reader to open harmful links or attachments or reveal personal information, often by impersonating a trusted sender and using urgent language; the reader should recognize the signs, not click, and report the message.

sourceRecords.title: RFC 5321: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol
sourceRecords.notes: Standards-track (October 2008). Authoritative definition that SMTP transfers/relays mail between servers and handles submission; supports the address local-part@domain form (mailbox = local-part @ domain) and the outgoing-transport claim. Read the RFC-Editor HTML copy.

sourceRecords.title: RFC 5322: Internet Message Format
sourceRecords.notes: Standards-track. Defines the header/body structure and the From, To, Cc, Bcc, Subject, Date fields; addr-spec = local-part '@' domain. Confirms To/Cc addresses are visible to all recipients and describes Bcc handling where the Bcc field is stripped from copies delivered to To/Cc recipients so blind recipients stay hidden. Read the RFC-Editor HTML copy.

sourceRecords.title: RFC 9051: Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) - Version 4rev2
sourceRecords.notes: Standards-track (August 2021). Abstract: IMAP4rev2 allows a client to access and manipulate messages on a server; supports mailbox management, searching, selective fetch, and resynchronization. Supports the claim that IMAP keeps mail on the server and syncs across devices/folders. Read the RFC-Editor HTML copy.

sourceRecords.title: RFC 1939: Post Office Protocol - Version 3
sourceRecords.notes: Internet Standard (STD 53, May 1996). Lets a workstation retrieve mail from a server maildrop; typical model is download-then-delete, and it is explicitly not intended for extensive server-side manipulation (contrasted with the more advanced IMAP). Supports the POP-vs-IMAP contrast. Read the RFC-Editor HTML copy.

sourceRecords.title: Recognize and Report Phishing
sourceRecords.notes: U.S. government guidance. Phishing tries to get you to open harmful links/attachments or reveal personal/financial info, often via a message impersonating a trusted party with urgent language or lookalike addresses; advice is recognize, resist (don't click), report, delete. Used only as the handoff pointer to the dedicated Phishing topic. Fetched via curl with a browser user-agent (direct WebFetch returned 403).
